advisory.title: Use-after-free from a comparator that answers inconsistently
advisory.description:
`OrderedSkipList`, `SkipSet` and `SkipMap` can free a node that is still
linked when a `Comparator` or `Ord` implementation gives different answers for
the same pair of values during one mutating call. A later call reads the freed
memory (CWE-416). A safe `impl Ord` with the default comparator is enough to
reach it.

The mutating traversals record a precursor at each level: the last node whose
link points at a node comparing not-`Less` than the target. The splice code
assumes every recorded precursor's link points at or past the final position.
If a later comparison reports one of those nodes as `Less`, the walk steps
past it and the assumption breaks. Removals such as `take_first`, `take` and
`remove` then rewire the wrong link and free the target while its real
predecessor still points at it. `insert` builds crossed links and wrong skip
distances from the same precursors.

A comparator that is a pure function of its two arguments cannot trigger
this, even if it is not transitive. The trigger is a stateful or
non-deterministic implementation, for example one that reads a counter, a
cache, a clock or a random source.

The flaw was corrected in 1.3.0. The mutating traversals track the link target
of the lowest recorded precursor and panic with "comparator does not implement
a total order" when a `Less` answer contradicts an earlier one. Every splice
site also checks its precursors before the first write. Each detected
contradiction panics before any link, value or length changes, so the
collection stays valid and safe to drop.

advisory.title: Aliasing violations in splice, mutable iteration and cursors
advisory.description:
Four code paths create a pointer whose permission is later revoked, then
write through it. Miri reports each as undefined behaviour under both the
Tree Borrows and Stacked Borrows aliasing models (CWE-758). All four are
reachable from safe code with standard `Ord` types.

1. **Splice back-pointer.** `split_off`, `split_off_index` and `append` stored
   the first spliced node's `prev` pointer from a reference to the head, then
   wrote through that same reference, invalidating the stored pointer. A later
   `pop_first` or `pop_front` writes through it. This affects all four
   collections.
2. **`SkipMap::range_mut` back pointer.** With an `Included` or `Excluded`
   upper bound, the back pointer came from a shared reference. `next_back`
   hands out `&mut V` through it, and writing to that value is undefined
   behaviour.
3. **`IterMut::next_back` reads a yielded node.** In `SkipList` and `SkipMap`,
   `next_back` read the predecessor node even after the front end had yielded
   it as `&mut`. The read freezes the caller's reference, and the caller's
   next write through it is undefined behaviour. This affects `iter_mut`,
   `values_mut` and `range_mut` used from both ends.
4. **Cursor list pointer.** `lower_bound_mut` and `upper_bound_mut` on
   `OrderedSkipList` and `SkipSet` (`cursor` feature) took the cursor's list
   pointer, then searched through `&self`. A comparator with interior-mutable
   state, such as a `Cell` call counter, wrote to the list's memory through
   that shared borrow and invalidated the cursor's pointer. The comparator can
   be a fully consistent order. `SkipMap` cursors are not affected.

No miscompilation has been observed in an optimised build. A future compiler
may still optimise on the violated aliasing assumptions.

The flaws were corrected in 1.3.0. Each fix derives the pointer used for
mutation from the collection's long-lived allocation pointers, and each has a
Miri regression test.

advisory.title: Use-after-free in `clear` and `retain` when an element's `Drop` panics
advisory.description:
`SkipList::clear` drops the node chain and only then resets `tail` and `len`.
The drop runs each element's `Drop`, and `T` carries no bounds excluding a
panicking one. If it unwinds, `tail` still points at the freed node while `len`
stays non-zero.

`back()`, `back_mut()`, `last_key_value()` and `last()` dereference `tail`
through `unsafe`, so reading the container after the unwind is a use-after-free
(CWE-416). `Drop for SkipList` calls `Box::from_raw` on `self.head`, which
`clear` already destroyed, so dropping the container is a double free
(CWE-415).

`retain`, `retain_mut` and `dedup_by` reach the same state through
`Node::filter_rebuild`, which frees nodes and runs a user predicate before the
caller commits `tail` and `len`. There the head links are left partially
rewired, so traversal can also reach freed nodes.

## Mitigation

Update to 1.1.1.
